Solution:
Let G be a directed graph. Define the transitive closure GT as the directed
graph sharing the same vertex set as G, where an edge u →v exists in GT if and only if
there is a directed path from u to v in G. Furthermore, define a transitive reduction of G to
be a graph with the minimum number of edges such that its transitive closure is identical to
GT. Given that a graph may generally admit multiple transitive reductions, prove that G
possesses a unique transitive reduction if and only if G is acyclic.
Solution.
We work with finite directed graphs (digraphs), with no parallel edges; a directed path
is a sequence of vertices of positive length with all edges oriented consistently along the
sequence.
For a digraph G = (V, E), its transitive closure GT is the digraph on V with edge set
ET = {(u, v) ∈V × V : there is a directed path u ⇝v in G}.
A transitive reduction of G is a digraph H = (V, F) with the minimum possible number of
edges such that HT = GT.
We begin with the classical part of the statement, valid for acyclic graphs.
Theorem 1 (DAG case). If G is acyclic, then G has a unique transitive reduction.
